You get told remote work is a win for everybody. I've mentored five junior engineers for the last two years and it isn't. They don't need tickets, docs, or a set of scheduled meetings. What they need is to get in on design arguments, watch somebody else get through a nasty bug, and get answers before a little uncertainty snowballs. You get all of that for free in an office. Work from home and they have to figure out when to interrupt, get a call set up, and explain a problem they probably don't get yet. That is a pretty steep thing to ask of someone who hasn't had the chance to learn it.

I've watched that setup screw up feedback. A short note on a code review ends up reading like a final judgment, and the lag on getting answers kills any forward motion. The people I worked with moved ahead a lot quicker when they could pair up in person, work through things on a whiteboard, and actually get hold of the seniors. None of this means you should scrap flexibility. It works fine for people who can direct their own efforts. For a beginner, being around other people is what gets them there. It is how they pick up the confidence, context, and judgment they are going to need. You are going to end up with weaker technical leadership down the road if you just hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar.

A float valve keeps a livestock water trough filled using a simple mechanical feedback loop. The valve is connected to a pressurized water supply line. A buoyant float, typically made of hollow plastic, rests on the water’s surface and is attached to a hinged lever arm. 

When livestock drink and the water level drops, the float sinks. This movement pulls the lever down, opening the valve and allowing fresh water to flow into the trough. As the incoming water level rises, the buoyant float rides upward. This upward motion lifts the lever arm, which gradually pushes a plunger or seal back into the valve inlet. Once the water reaches the designated fill line, the lever forces the valve completely shut, stopping the flow.

Two ordinary causes of trough overflow are physical obstructions and mechanical wear. Debris, such as algae, dirt, or ice, can get wedged in the valve seat, preventing it from sealing completely. Alternatively, the float itself can develop a puncture, filling with water and sinking to the bottom, which keeps the valve permanently open.

Remote work is heralded as the panacea. From my two years of mentoring 5 junior engineers, it's overblown for any juniors still learning how to code.

Jrs don't need tickets or documentation or meeting. They need to sit in on design conversations. They need to see how others debug issues. They need to ask questions before they have hours of confusion. That kind of interaction happens organically in an office. For remote work, they need to know the right times to cut in, set up a call, and to explain a problem that they might not even fully understand yet. It's a skill (and a tough one!) to have before you have a chance to learn it.

I've seen the feedback issues in remote work. Short comments on code review can feel like the final word instead of a learning opportunity. Also, it takes longer, so less momentum. The jrs I mentored typically improved faster if they had in person pairing, whiteboard sessions, etc. and had easy access to seniors.

I'm not trying to push for offices or anti-flexibility. Remote work can be great for self-driven devs. But for jrs, proximity is a booster that gives confidence, context, and instincts. Sending jrs off with a laptop and a calendar can be a drag on junior development which can result in less good technical leadership in the future.

A float valve keeps a livestock trough filled by connecting a water supply line to a valve controlled by a buoyant float. The float rests on the water surface and is attached to a lever arm. When animals drink and the level drops, the float sinks, and the lever opens the valve so water flows in.

As the trough refills, the float rises with the surface. This motion gradually pushes the lever in the closing direction, pressing a seal against the valve seat. Once the water reaches the set height, the seal shuts completely and the flow stops. When the level falls again, the cycle repeats.

Two ordinary causes of overflow are:

1. **Debris or mineral buildup on the valve seat or seal.** Grit, algae, or scale can prevent a tight seal, so water keeps seeping in even when the float is fully raised.

2. **A misadjusted or damaged float assembly.** If the lever is bent, the float is cracked and waterlogged, or the shutoff height is set too high, the valve closes late or not at all.

A float valve maintains a consistent water level in a livestock trough by leveraging simple mechanical principles. The device consists of a buoyant float attached to a lever arm, which connects directly to a water inlet valve. When animals drink and the water level drops, the float descends with the surface. This downward motion pulls the lever arm, opening the valve and allowing fresh water to flow into the trough. As the trough refills, the rising water lifts the float back up. This upward movement gradually pushes the lever arm, slowly closing the valve until the water reaches the predetermined height, at which point the valve shuts completely, stopping the flow.

Despite this reliable design, overflow issues can occur. One common cause is debris accumulation. Dirt, algae, or mineral deposits can jam the valve mechanism, preventing it from sealing tightly even when the float is fully raised. Another frequent issue involves physical obstruction or damage to the float itself. If the float becomes waterlogged, it loses buoyancy and fails to rise properly. Alternatively, external objects like sticks or tangled vegetation might block the float’s path, stopping it from lifting the lever arm enough to shut off the water supply, leading to continuous running and eventual overflow.
